title: Book 4 — Melpomene, Chapter 10
paragraphs: Upon this he drew one of his bows—for up to that time Heracles, they say, used to carry two—and showed her the girdle; then he handed over both the bow and the girdle, which had a golden cup at the end of its clasp. Having given them, he departed. She, when her sons had been born and grown to manhood, first gave them names: one she called Agathyrsos, the next Gelonos, and the youngest Skythes. Then, remembering the charge given to her, she did as commanded. Two of her sons, Agathyrsos and Gelonos, proving unable to accomplish the task set before them, were cast out of the land by their mother. But Skythes, the youngest, performed the task and remained in the land; and from Skythes, son of Heracles, are descended, they say, the succeeding kings of the Scythians. They say also that it is because of the cup that the Scythians still to this day wear cups attached to their girdles—and this is the one thing his mother contrived for Skythes. Such is the story told by the Hellenes who dwell around the Pontus.
